name: The Black Mulberries of the Bishop's Palace

location.address: Palace lawns, The Bishop's Palace, Wells BA5 2PD

story:
Five black mulberries were planted in the Bishop's Palace gardens in 1897. Two of them are still here, and since 2001 they have had company. A third mulberry was given to Bishop Bickersteth as a present for his 80th birthday, so the Palace now has three, an old pair and a young one.

That makes the survivors about 130 years old, a figure that comes from the documented planting date rather than an estimate, which is rarer than it sounds for a tree in an English garden. Black mulberries tend to grow into low, broad, leaning crowns that look older than they are, so a known date is the useful thing to have.

They stand on the wide lawns of the Palace gardens, laid out as pleasure grounds by Bishop Law in 1825 and 1826, with the roofless ruins of the bishops' Great Hall behind them. The gardens are a Grade II registered landscape and an RHS partner garden, and the mulberries share the lawns with other specimen trees, among them a tulip tree that the Palace says is almost 200 years old.

No girth has been published for either of the old pair. In late summer the dark fruit ripens on the branches.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise the old pair by their low, broad crowns, two of the three black mulberries on the Palace lawns; the third, planted in 2001, is the young one. They stand on the wide lawns near the ruins of the Great Hall.

best_time.label: late August into September, when the dark mulberries ripen on the old pair

name: The Tulip Tree of the Bishop's Palace

location.address: Palace gardens, near the Great Hall lawn, The Bishop's Palace, Wells BA5 2PD

story:
By the Palace's own account, this tulip tree is almost 200 years old, a North American tree that has spent nearly two centuries growing beside the ruins of a medieval bishops' hall in Wells.

The setting was made for specimen trees. When Bishop Law remodelled the Palace gardens in 1825 and 1826, he laid out a great lawn planted with them where the south wall of the Great Hall had stood, with the ruins of the hall as its backdrop. The tulip tree's age fits that date. No record we have found names it among his plantings, though, so read the age as the owner's claim rather than a documented date.

Tulip trees are easy to pick out once you know the leaf. Each one is four-lobed with the tip cut off square, as if someone had taken scissors to it, a shape no native British tree has. In early summer the tree carries the cup-shaped flowers that give it its name, often high in the crown, and in autumn the whole tree turns gold and orange, which is when it stands out most clearly against the stone of the ruins.

The gardens are behind a ticket, and the Palace publishes no girth or height for the tree.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its leaves, four-lobed with the tip cut off square, turning gold and orange in autumn. It stands among the specimen trees on the great lawn near the ruins of the Great Hall.

best_time.label: October, when the squared-off leaves turn gold and orange against the ruins
